In mathematics, specifically [[category theory]], a '''pseudo-tensor category''' is a generalization of a [[symmetric monoidal category]] (also known as a tensor category) introduced by [[Alexander Beilinson|A. Beilinson]] and [[Drinfeld|V. Drinfeld]] in their book "Chiral algebras".

The notion can also be defined as a [[colored operad]] or [[multicategory]]. In particular, a pseudo-tensor category with a single object is the same as an [[operad]].

== Definition ==
A ''pseudo-tensor category'' ''C'' consists of the following data<ref>{{harvnb|Beilinson|Drinfeld|loc=1.1.1.}}</ref>
*A class of ''objects'',
*For each finite set <math>I</math>, each finite set of objects <math>X_i, i \in I</math> parametrized by <math>I</math> and another object <math>Y</math>, the set
*:<math>P_I(\{ X_i \}, Y),</math>
*For each surjective map <math>J \to I</math> between finite sets, finite sets of objects <math>\{ Y_i \}_{i \in I}, \{ X_j \}_{j \in J}</math> and an object ''Z'', the map
*:<math>\circ : P_I(\{ Y_i \}, Z) \times \prod_{i \in I} P_{\pi^{-1}(i)}(\{ X_j \}, Y_i) \to P_J(\{ X_j \}, Z),</math>
*For each object <math>X</math>, the element <math>\operatorname{id}_X</math> in <math>P_*(\{ X \}, X)</math> where * is a set with a single element,
subject to the associativity and the unitality axioms
*for surjective maps <math>K \to J</math> and <math>J \to I</math>, <math>\varphi \circ (\psi_i \circ \chi_j) = (\varphi \circ \psi_i) \circ \chi_j</math>,
*<math>\operatorname{id}_Y \circ \varphi = \varphi \circ \operatorname{id}_{X_i} = \varphi</math>.

Let ''C'' be a pseudo-tensor category. For given objects <math>X, Y</math>, let <math>\operatorname{Hom}(X, Y) = P_{*}(\{ X \}, Y)</math>. Then the class of objects in <math>C</math> together with Hom, <math>\circ</math> and the identities form a category. Thus, a pseudo-tensor category can be thought of as a category together with extra data. In particular, a category is the same thing as a pseudo-tensor category with <math>P_I = \emptyset, \# I > 1</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Beilinson|Drinfeld|loc=1.1.2.}}</ref>

On the other extreme, a pseudo-tensor category with a single object is the same as an [[operad]].<ref>{{harvnb|Beilinson|Drinfeld|loc=1.1.4.}}</ref> Indeed, a category with a single object is a monoid (unital semigroup) and thus a pseudo-tensor category with a single is like a monoid but with various n-ary operators. A finite set <math>\{ X_i \}_{i \in I}</math> in the definition of a pseudo-tensor is an ''unordered'' finite set. This amounts to the invariance under a symmetric group in the definition of an operad.

Finally, let ''C'' be a symmetric monoidal category. Then let
:<math>P_I(\{ X_i \}, Y) = \operatorname{Hom}(\otimes_{i \in I} X_i, Y),</math>
which is well-defined since ''C'' is symmetric. The symmetric-monoidal structure include coherent isomorphisms
:<math>\otimes_{j \in J} X_j \overset{\sim}\to \otimes_{i \in I} (\otimes_{j \in \pi^{-1}(i)} X_j)</math>
which gives <math>\circ</math> in the definition of a pseudo-tensor category. Conversely, a pseudo-tensor category with such <math>\otimes_{i \in I} X_i</math> and coherent isomorphisms defines a symmetric monoidal category. In this way, a pseudo-tensor category generalizes a symmetric monoidal category.<ref>{{harvnb|Beilinson|Drinfeld|loc=1.1.3.}}</ref>

In the definition, we can drop the symmetry requirement; namely, instead of a finite set of objects, we can use a finite sequence of objects. In this case, we get the notion of a [[multicategory]]. In other words, a pseudo-tensor category is (essentially) a symmetric multicategory.

== Linear case ==
Like an [[enriched category]], a pseudo-tensor category can also be defined over a symmetric monoidal category ''V''; namely, we require <math>P_I</math> as well as <math>\circ</math> take values in ''V'' instead of the category of sets in the definition. A particularly important case is when ''V'' is the category of vector spaces; i.e., the images of <math>P_I</math> are sets of multilinear maps and if tensor product is available,
:<math>P_I(\{X_i\}, Y) = \operatorname{Hom}(\otimes_{i \in I} X_i, Y).</math>
